newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Foncier swings into profit in first half.
newsitem.headline: Credit Foncier swings into profit in first half.

text.p: Property lender Credit Foncier de France, which suffered huge losses as a result of a collapse in property prices, reported on Friday a surprise 402 million franc ($79.3 million) first half net attributable profit.

The profit compared with a 12 million franc loss in the same year-earlier period and Credit Foncier, due to be taken over by a state bank and then wound down, forecast a "positive" full year-result barring a fresh downturn in the property market.

Until recently the bank had been widely expected to post a loss of 520 million francs. But in recent days French newspapers had reported the bank would be in profit. Trading in its shares were indefinitely suspended on August 28.
The results included provisions of 671 million francs, sharply down from the 1.3 billion francs it reported for the same year earlier period.
Credit Foncier, France's second biggest bond issuer after the state, said net banking income fell four percent to 2.2 billion francs while operating profit was stable at 975 million.
First-half profits were swelled by an exceptional gain of 96.9 million francs on the sale of municipal debt and capital gains of 37.3 million francs on sale of investment holdings.
The government announced in July that Credit Foncier would be taken over by state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC) before a "managed wind-down" of the bank.
The move came after Credit Foncier reported losses of 10.8 billion francs for 1995 that included 13.6 billion francs worth of provisions for property losses.
French newspapers have said a profit could have repercussions for the CDC offer being made on behalf of the government at a price of 70 francs a share.

Last year's accounts have been contested by one shareholder action group, Adam, which say the 1995 provisions were too big and have demanded at least 100 francs a share in any state-orchestrated buyout.

The group, which was also hit by loss of its monopoly to sell low-cost mortgages, is private but its top management is controlled by the government due to its status as a "specialised financial institution".
The takeover, which will cost in the neighbourhood of 2.5 billion francs, has yet to be executed and requires acceptances covering two-thirds of the shares in the group.
